summary_paragraph: A man with a history of non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 20%), type I diabetes, schizophrenia, and prior crack cocaine use was admitted for acute on chronic systolic heart failure presenting with severe respiratory distress. He reported worsening dyspnea on exertion, orthopnea, and PND over three days, with no fever but chills and a dry cough. In the ED, he was hypoxic (82% on room air), tachypneic, and tachycardic, with immediate improvement on BIPAP. Labs showed elevated proBNP (4687), normal troponin, and no infection on blood or urine cultures. Chest X-ray revealed bilateral airspace opacities, slightly worse than prior. He was treated with IV furosemide for aggressive diuresis, leading to significant symptomatic improvement. Antibiotics were discontinued after no evidence of infection. His diabetes was managed with insulin adjustments after steroid-induced hyperglycemia. Schizophrenia was addressed with outpatient psychiatry follow-up recommended due to persistent auditory hallucinations. He stabilized, ambulated independently, and was discharged home on his prior medications with instructions on daily weight monitoring and low-sodium diet.
